routes.description: Establish that the Christian account integrates divine hiddenness, suffering, conscious personal reality, objective morality, and historical moral development through the incarnate and cruciform narrative of God and humanity.
routes.successCriteria: Show that distinctively Christian commitments supply a coherent comparative explanation across the motion's domains, including principled replies to hiddenness and evil and an account of moral truth, motivation, and progress.

motionBridge.description: Connect the Christian narrative's treatment of God, persons, suffering, goodness, and history to a comparatively unified account of all principal domains in the motion.

centralBridges.description: Explain how divine presence can coexist with felt absence and how incarnation and the forsaken Christ constitute personal revelation within human estrangement.
Explain why suffering is compatible with Christian theism by relating human epistemic limits to divine participation, judgment, and resurrection hope.
Connect conscious, rational, interpersonal experience to an ultimate personal reality while distinguishing omnipresence from personal encounter.
Ground objective goodness and obligation in divine relational life and show how the Jesus-centered scriptural narrative can guide moral formation and development through history.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for variations in religious awareness through inherited intellectual and cultural conditions without making individual vice the sole explanation.
Explain how enduring moral principles can acquire new applications when historical or technological conditions reveal previously unresolved problems.

routes.description: Establish that hiddenness and suffering create unresolved tensions for Christian theism and that agnostic, realist, constructivist, or anti-realist alternatives can explain relevant features without the full Christian account.
routes.successCriteria: Show either that Christian explanations conflict with expected divine love and intelligibility or that competing accounts remain adequate for consciousness, morality, motivation, and moral change, defeating the claimed comparative advantage.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that Christian theism does not secure a sufficiently coherent or distinctive explanatory advantage across the motion's principal domains.

centralBridges.description: Derive an expectation of accessible relationship from perfect divine love and test resistance and cultural explanations against sincere, committed, and geographically varied cases.
Press the evidential force of apparently gratuitous suffering and determine whether appeals to inscrutable reasons undermine other claims about divine goodness and purpose.
Distinguish openness to consciousness or nonphysical reality from evidence for the specifically personal divine agent asserted by Christian theism.
Test whether theism uniquely grounds moral truth and motivation and whether Christian moral development has non-retrospective criteria for separating progress from corruption.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use demographic, believer, and rival-faith cases to test whether culpable resistance adequately tracks the distribution of experienced revelation.
Explain moral consensus, disagreement, and motivation partly through affective and narrative cultural formation available beyond a uniquely Christian framework.

sections.title: Divine Love, Hiddenness, and Accessible Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether perfect relational love predicts clearer divine availability and whether resistance, cultural mediation, scripture, incarnation, and divine solidarity can explain persistent or uneven experiences of absence.

sections.title: Evil, Divine Participation, and Inscrutable Reasons
sections.rationale: The treatment of severe suffering bears directly on the comparative account: it requires examining both epistemic humility about divine reasons and the Christian claim that God personally bears suffering and promises resurrection.

sections.title: Consciousness and the Inference to Personal Divine Reality
sections.rationale: The motion requires distinguishing the existence and character of conscious interpersonal experience from the further inference to a personal God, while assessing the Christian account of ubiquitous presence and incarnate encounter.

sections.title: Moral Truth, Obligation, and Motivation
sections.rationale: This issue compares Trinitarian and divine-command approaches to objective goodness and obligation with realist, constructivist, and affective anti-realist alternatives, including their respective accounts of practical moral motivation.

sections.title: Christian Narrative and Criteria for Moral Progress
sections.rationale: The historical claim requires explaining Christianity's relation to human dignity and moral formation while testing whether scripture, the image of God, and the cruciform narrative provide usable criteria for distinguishing development from corruption.
